# Config audit
`circleci config audit` checks a pipeline config for supply-chain and secret-handling
risks: untrusted input reaching a shell, unpinned dependencies, secrets in the file,
and contexts handed to every branch. It runs offline and reads only the file you give
it. With `--online` it also reads project, org and context settings, using GET requests
only; it never changes anything in your organization.

Orbs are not expanded, so findings inside an orb's own commands and jobs are not
reported. Only the config in the file is audited.

Each finding has a severity (how much it matters) and a confidence (how likely it is to
be a real problem).

## Rules

The Needs column says what a rule audits: the config file, or project, org and context
settings, which are read only with `--online`.

| Rule | Severity | Confidence | Catches | Needs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `pipeline-value-injection` | high | high | Pipeline value an outsider controls is expanded into a shell command | file |
| `unpinned-orb` | medium | high | Orb reference is not pinned to an exact version | file |
| `unpinned-image` | medium | high | Docker image is not pinned to a digest | file |
| `cache-poisoning` | medium | low | A cache any branch can fill is restored by a job with secrets or on the default branch | file |
| `ssh-keys-unrestricted` | medium | high | add_ssh_keys does not name the keys to add | file |
| `curl-pipe-shell` | medium | medium | A downloaded script is piped straight into a shell | file |
| `hardcoded-secret` | high | medium | A secret is written into the config as a literal value | file |
| `context-on-any-branch` | medium | medium | A workflow job gets a context on every branch | file |
| `dynamic-config-untrusted` | low | low | A setup workflow continues with a config that is generated, or not checked in | file |
| `fork-pr-secrets` | high | high | Fork pull requests are built and receive project secrets | `--online` |
| `ssh-rerun-allowed` | medium | high | Jobs can be rerun with SSH | `--online` |
| `settings-not-admin-only` | low | high | Project settings can be changed by non-admins | `--online` |
| `user-checkout-keys-allowed` | low | high | User checkout keys are allowed in the org | `--online` |
| `uncertified-orbs-allowed` | low | high | Uncertified public orbs are allowed in the org | `--online` |
| `context-unrestricted` | medium | high | A context the config uses has no project or expression restriction | `--online` |

### pipeline-value-injection

Values such as the branch name, tag or commit message are chosen by whoever pushes or opens a pull request. Expanded into a run step before the shell reads it, they become shell syntax, so a crafted branch name runs commands with the job's secrets.

Fix: pass it through environment: (BRANCH: << pipeline.git.branch >>) and use "$BRANCH"

### unpinned-orb

A major-version alias, no version or @volatile lets the orb publisher change the code your jobs run, with your secrets, without a change to your config.

Fix: pin the orb to an exact version (name@X.Y.Z)

### unpinned-image

A tag can be moved to different content at any time, so a job can silently run an image you never reviewed. :latest and a missing tag are the most exposed.

Fix: pin the image to a digest (image:tag@sha256:<digest>)

### cache-poisoning

Without {{ .Branch }} in the key, a build of any branch, including one from an outside contributor, can save a cache that the default branch or a job with a context later restores, so planted files run with its secrets.

Fix: add {{ .Branch }} to the cache key so a branch cannot fill a cache that other branches restore

### ssh-keys-unrestricted

Without fingerprints, every SSH key added to the project is loaded into the job, so a compromised step can use keys the job never needed.

Fix: list the keys to add with fingerprints: [<fingerprint>]

### curl-pipe-shell

The script runs unreviewed and unverified, so whoever controls the server, or a network position in between, runs code in your job with its secrets.

Fix: download the script, verify its checksum, then run it

### hardcoded-secret

The config is readable by everyone with access to the repository and lives forever in its history, so a literal token or password there has to be treated as leaked.

Fix: move the value to a context or project environment variable

### context-on-any-branch

A context's secrets are handed to the job on whichever branch runs it, so anyone who can push a branch can write a config change that reads them.

Fix: add filters.branches.only, an approval job, or a restricted context

### dynamic-config-untrusted

The config reviewed is a setup config for a dynamic pipeline. Review the config used to continue the pipeline.

Fix: continue with a config checked into the repository, or check what the step generates before continuing

### fork-pr-secrets

With both "Build forked pull requests" and "Pass secrets to builds from forked pull requests" on, anyone who can open a pull request from a fork can change the config of their copy and read the project's environment variables and contexts. This applies to OAuth pipelines; GitHub App pipelines never build fork pull requests.

Fix: turn off "Pass secrets to builds from forked pull requests" in Project Settings > Advanced

### ssh-rerun-allowed

Anyone who can rerun a job can open a shell in it, with every secret the job holds, so SSH reruns widen who can read the project's secrets.

Fix: disable SSH reruns for this project

### settings-not-admin-only

Settings such as the fork pull request options and SSH reruns decide who can reach the project's secrets. Letting any member change them lets any member loosen them.

Fix: require admin access to change this project's settings

### user-checkout-keys-allowed

A user key acts as the person who created it, so a job using one can reach every repository that person can, well beyond the project it runs for.

Fix: disable user checkout keys in the org's settings

### uncertified-orbs-allowed

Any published orb can then run in your jobs, with their secrets, although CircleCI has not reviewed it. The finding is medium when the config also has an unpinned orb.

Fix: turn off uncertified public orbs in the org's settings, and pin every orb to an exact version

### context-unrestricted

A context with no restriction, or only one for a group such as All members, is open to every branch of every project in the org, and does not stop fork pull requests from receiving it.

Fix: restrict the context to this project or to an expression such as the default branch

## Suppressing a finding

Put a comment on the flagged line, or alone on the line directly above it:

```yaml
- run: curl -fsSL https://example.com/install.sh | sh # circleci-audit: ignore[curl-pipe-shell]
# circleci-audit: ignore[unpinned-image, unpinned-orb]
- image: cimg/node:lts
```

Separate several rule ids with commas. An id that names no rule is reported as a
warning, and a known id that does not match the finding suppresses nothing.

The comment also works inside a `run: |` block, where a shell comment on the line above a
command annotates that exact command; the shell ignores it. Suppressed findings do not
change the exit code, and are counted as suppressed in the summary.

Settings findings from `--online` have no line to carry a comment, so a comment cannot
suppress them. Raise `--min-severity` to leave them out.

## Exit codes

- 0: nothing at or above `--min-severity` (default low), or only suppressed findings.
- 7: one or more findings at or above `--min-severity`. The report is still written in full
  to stdout; the error goes to stderr.
- 2: the file could not be read or parsed, or a flag was invalid.

With `--online`, a missing token, an unresolvable project or a failed request is a warning:
the offline rules still run, and the exit code is not affected.

## Code scanning

`--format sarif` writes a SARIF 2.1.0 log to stdout, which GitHub code scanning and other
SARIF consumers can ingest. Suppressed findings are included, marked as suppressed. A
SARIF upload needs a file path, not stdin, so write the log to a file and audit a file
path rather than `-` so locations point at the file in your repository. The audit exits 7
when it finds something, so keep the job going with `|| true` and let the upload step
report the findings.

A CircleCI job that writes the file (it assumes the circleci CLI is installed):

```yaml
jobs:
  audit-config:
    docker:
      - image: cimg/base:current
    steps:
      - checkout
      - run:
          name: Audit pipeline config
          command: circleci config audit --format sarif > audit.sarif || true
      - store_artifacts:
          path: audit.sarif
```

Then upload `audit.sarif` with the code scanning upload step of your choice, for example the
GitHub CLI or the code scanning REST API.
